title: Atomisation in Literacy
author: fivetwelvethirteen
summary: This piece from fivetwelvethirteen lays out atomisation, a technique borrowed from math instruction, and argues for its careful, limited application in literacy teaching. The author frames the distinction with an analogy: math is mostly a 'ladder' where concepts build in sequence, while literacy is mostly a 'spiderweb' where the connections between ideas matter more than any single sequence, so atomisation, breaking a skill into a small chunk taught in isolation, only cleanly fits the ladder-like parts of literacy instruction. Using a personal-narrative unit as a worked example, the author shows how confusion over 'first person' undermined a definition until that prerequisite concept was isolated and taught with mini-whiteboards before being folded back into the larger idea. The piece's real contribution is the three-step cycle 'atomise, retrieve, expand': after isolating a concept, students must retrieve it on a spaced schedule to move it into long-term memory, and then the teacher must deliberately reapply it across new contexts so the atom doesn't stay disconnected from everything else students know. The author closes with a direct critique of educational technology's implicit assumption that mapping every atom and its relationships precisely enough could mechanize teaching, arguing that most of literacy learning resists that kind of clean decomposition.
points: The author distinguishes 'ladder' subjects (like math, where concepts build sequentially) from 'spiderweb' subjects (like literacy, where connections matter more than sequence), arguing atomisation only cleanly fits the ladder parts.

A concrete classroom example, teaching 'first person' before 'personal narrative', shows atomisation's core mechanism: isolate the prerequisite concept and teach it alone before it's needed inside a more complex idea.
The three-step cycle 'atomise, retrieve, expand' is offered as the necessary complement to isolation: retrieval schedules the atom into long-term memory, and expansion reconnects it to new contexts.
The piece warns that atomisation without expansion risks turning curriculum into disconnected trivia, since literacy's value lies mostly in the web of connections between ideas.
It closes with a critique of ed-tech's implicit theory of learning: that mapping every atom and its relationships precisely enough could let a machine sequence perfect instruction.
quotes: Atomisation is a reasonably intuitive idea in math class. Break a math skill into small chunks, teach one chunk at a time, and build bit by bit toward larger ideas.
The key insight of atomisation is that it's hard to learn two things at the same time. If students don't know what "first person" means, that definition up there won't make much sense.
Next up, I want students to retrieve that atom. This is where that learning moves securely into long-term memory.

The most important step of this whole thing is expansion. Expansion means I want to expand the contexts in which students are using this knowledge. One risk of atomisation is that breaking learning down into small steps means those steps become isolated.

Atomise, retrieve, expand," is my reminder: atomisation is useful, but only if students retain the atom and apply it in lots of different ways. Atomisation alone risks turning the curriculum into a bunch of isolated, disconnected bits of knowledge.

It's tempting to believe that, if only we could identify all the little atoms and relationships between them, we could build a machine to teach all those little atoms in the right order and make sure every student learns. That's the dream of lots of education technology right now.
